claims.claim: OpenStax's Introduction to Anthropology defines a family as two or more people in an adaptable social and economic alliance that involves kinship, whether perceived through blood, marriage, or another permanent or semipermanent arrangement; it frequently, but not always, involves reproduction, the care of offspring, and coresidence within the same locale.

Britannica defines a family as a group of persons united by the ties of marriage, blood, or adoption, constituting a single household and interacting with each other in their respective social positions, usually those of spouses, parents, and children.

Family is a sociocultural construct: which people count as family is defined and recognized differently across cultures according to differing social norms, and the definition a group endorses reflects kinship ideas, cultural traditions, and socioemotional ties rather than biology alone.

Family is universal across human societies in the sense that every society recognizes families, but its forms vary: anthropologists have defined basic family types that are duplicated across cultures with minor variations, and families vary greatly across cultures and adapt to changing social and economic needs.

A household is a group of individuals who live within the same residence and share socioeconomic needs associated with production and consumption; a family and a household may be the same unit but do not have to be — families can live within larger households containing two or more families, and family members can be physically separated while working or studying elsewhere.

A nuclear family is composed of one or two parents and their immediate offspring; it is the smallest family structure and is often found in societies where geographic mobility is valued, from small-scale foraging bands to industrial and market societies.

An extended family includes two or more family units functioning as a single integrated family, may involve three or more generations or married siblings living together (joint families), and is the most common type of family worldwide.

Some societies organize families around mothers: among the Mosuo of China, women form sexual alliances with men from outside their families and remain with their brothers in their own households to raise their children, who belong to the women's lineage; among the Mundurucú of lowland Amazonia, the resident family is a mother and her preadolescent offspring while the father resides in the tribal men's house.

Families can include fictive kin — people defined as family regardless of biology, based on intentional relationships such as adoption, godparenthood (compadrazgo), or intimate personal ties — so family membership is not limited to blood or marriage.

Families perform care and socialization functions: Britannica reports that the family rears and socializes children, cares for its members when they are sick or disabled, and provides emotional and psychological security; economically it provides food, shelter, clothing, and physical security for members too young or too old to provide for themselves, and OpenStax's definition of family as a social and economic alliance and of the household as a unit of production and consumption captures the same economic cooperation.

The two-parent nuclear household has become less typical in the United States over the last several generations: as of the 2016 US census, 69 percent of US children under 18 lived in a two-parent household, down from 88 percent in 1960, while the share living in female single-headed households rose from 8 percent in 1960 to 23 percent in 2016.

Family types are adaptive: each type is adapted to the social and economic needs of the family unit and is normally associated with particular subsistence strategies, and the family unit is a remarkably adaptive cultural mechanism (OpenStax chapter 11 summary likewise describes the family as those believed to be related with distinct rights and responsibilities, embedded within the larger kinship structure).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is the nuclear family the oldest or default family form in history?
positions: Britannica's family article states that the nuclear family 'is believed to be the oldest of the various types of families in existence.'

OpenStax's Introduction to Anthropology reports that worldwide the extended family is the most common type of family, that family types are adaptive mechanisms tied to social and economic needs, and that in the United States the two-parent nuclear household has declined from 88 percent of children under 18 in 1960 to 69 percent in 2016.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the honest note factually, per the assignment and per OpenStax's evidence: the nuclear family is one form among several, not the default of history. Britannica's 'oldest' claim is recorded here as a contested historical belief and is not asserted in the lesson; the lesson attributes the census figures and the 'most common worldwide' claim to OpenStax.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is family a universal institution if its forms vary so widely?
positions: Anthropology treats family as universal: OpenStax describes basic family types 'duplicated across cultures with minor variations' and family as embedded in kinship, a foundational social structure in every society.

Because family is a sociocultural construct defined differently across cultures, some scholars emphasize that the term itself is contested and that no single definition fits all cases (OpenStax notes family is difficult to categorize because of its diversity).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states universality factually — every society recognizes some group of people as family — while emphasizing variation, which is exactly what both OpenStax passages support. It does not claim uniformity of form, and it presents the diversity of definitions as part of the concept.

sourceRecords.title: 11.2 Defining Family and Household — Introduction to Anthropology (OpenStax)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A anchor (per subject source-map). OpenStax blocks direct fetch; read via Wayback Machine capture 20221002062723 of the canonical URL. Supports: the working definition of family ('two or more people in an adaptable social and economic alliance that involves kinship, whether perceived through blood, marriage, or other permanent or semipermanent arrangement'); the definition of household and the family/household distinction (families within larger households; families separated by migration); family as a sociocultural construct; nuclear, extended, and blended family types; the extended family as the most common family type worldwide; fictive kin and compadrazgo; mother-centered arrangements among the Mosuo of China and the Mundurucú of Brazil; US census figures on two-parent households (69% of children under 18 in 2016 vs 88% in 1960; female single-headed households 23% vs 8%). Facts synthesized into original prose; lesson examples are original.

sourceRecords.title: Ch. 11 Key Terms — Introduction to Anthropology (OpenStax)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A anchor. Read via Wayback Machine capture 20221007052052 of the canonical URL. Chapter glossary supporting the vocabulary and question bank: household ('a group of individuals who live within the same residence and share socioeconomic needs associated with production and consumption'); nuclear family ('a family composed of two parents and their immediate offspring'); extended family ('two or more family units functioning as a single integrated family; may involve two or more generations'); consanguineal tie (perceived biological connection, drawn as a single line on kinship charts); affinal tie (contractual relationship by marriage or mutual agreement, drawn as a double line); fictive kin ('a kinship tie that is socially interpreted to be by blood or marriage and that is based on intentional relationships, such as adoption, godparenthood, or intimate personal ties'); family of orientation and family of procreation. Vocabulary definitions in the lesson are original prose informed by this glossary.
